fr:title.text: Pi types in displayed categories require Conduché fibrations

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Pi types in displayed categories require Conduché fibrations

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Displayed categories model parts of a dependent type theory. Categories are contexts; displayed categories are dependent types.

html:ul.html:li: C^{\mathtt {D}} : \mathsf {Category}^{\mathtt {D}}\, C corresponds to C \vdash C^{\mathtt {D}}\ \mathsf {Type}.
\int C^{\mathtt {D}} : \mathsf {Category} corresponds to C, x : C^{\mathtt {D}}\ \mathsf {Ctx} — this is the total category.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Many of the operations of dependent type theory transfer cleanly to the displayed-category side. But Max claims that in general we cannot form a Pi type unless the associated displayed category is a Conduché fibration. Is this true, and if so, why?

A \Pi -type along a display map C^{\mathtt {D}} \to C is, categorically, a right adjoint to the substitution/pullback functor that reindexes displayed objects along that projection. So existence of \Pi -types is existence of a right adjoint to {\mathopen {}\left (-\right )\mathclose {}} \times _{C} \int C^{\mathtt {D}} on the slice — equivalently, exponentiability of the projection \int C^{\mathtt {D}} \to C viewed as an arrow in \mathbf {Cat}.

Conduché's theorem. A functor p : E \to B is exponentiable in \mathbf {Cat} iff it is a Conduché fibration: for every morphism u : e \to e' in E and every factorization p{\mathopen {}\left (u\right )\mathclose {}} = g \circ f in B, there exists an essentially unique factorization u = v \circ w in E with p{\mathopen {}\left (w\right )\mathclose {}} = f and p{\mathopen {}\left (v\right )\mathclose {}} = g.

fr:title.text: Why the weaker classes don't suffice

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Why the weaker classes don't suffice

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Cloven (Grothendieck) fibrations give \Pi -types when they are closed under dependent products in a stronger sense (i.e. they are \Pi -fibrations in the Jacobs sense, [jacobs-1999] Ch.~9). Generic displayed categories are weaker than fibrations, and even fibrations do not automatically give exponentiability of the total projection. Conduché is precisely the condition that fixes this for the underlying functor in \mathbf {Cat}.

Concretely, the Conduché condition lets us lift factorizations of substitutions in the base to factorizations of morphisms upstairs. Building a generic element of \Pi x{:}A.\, B requires assembling, for each substitution \sigma : \Gamma ' \to \Gamma , a coherent family of sections over A{\mathopen {}\llbracket \sigma \rrbracket \mathclose {}}; checking that two such families agree under further substitution requires matching up factorizations on the nose. This is exactly what fails without Conduché.

html:ul.html:li: Track down the precise statement and reference. Streicher's Fibered Categories à la Bénabou and Jacobs's Categorical Logic and Type Theory are the obvious sources.
Conduché's original paper (1972) for exponentiability = Conduché-fibration.

Reconcile with the standard display map / comprehension category presentations: in those settings \Pi -types are usually stipulated by asking the relevant pullback functor to have a right adjoint, which implicitly imposes exponentiability when one tries to construct examples in \mathbf {Cat}.
Confirm with Max that "in general we cannot have a Pi type" means "existence of \Pi -types in the resulting displayed type theory forces Conduché on the projection", not the reverse implication.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: This book is an attempt to give a systematic presentation of both logic and type theory from a categorical perspective, using the unifying concept of fibred category. Its intended audience consists of logicians, type theorists, category theorists and (theoretical) computer scientists.

Given a displayed category \overline {\mathcal {C}} over a category \mathcal {C} and another displayed category \overline {\mathcal {D}} over \int \overline {\mathcal {C}}, the total category of \overline {\mathcal {C}}, we can define \overline {\int } \overline {\mathcal {D}}, the displayed total category of \overline {\mathcal {D}}, as a displayed category over \mathcal {C}.
